newsitem.title: USA: Clinton experiences pain after surgery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton experiences pain after surgery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton experienced pain on Saturday as he recovered from surgery to repair a torn knee tendon but hoped to end his hospital stay on Sunday, a spokesman said.

After first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton led a physical therapist on a tour of the White House, workers were busy preparing the executive mansion for the return of a president using crutches -- moving furniture and using tape to fasten rugs, aides said.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton experienced "a fair amount of pain" during his first day following surgery at Bethesda National Naval Medical Centre in suburban Maryland.
"He's doing well with his recovery ... experiencing pain is normal," McCurry said, noting that Clinton was taking two non-narcotic pain killers to ease his discomfort.
Mindful of an upcoming summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday, Clinton was anxious to return to the White House on Sunday, McCurry said.
"He really wants to go home tomorrow and plans to go home tomorrow," McCurry said at a late Saturday afternoon briefing.
Clinton was described as being in an upbeat mood, despite his pain. "He's doing very well ... He's in excellent spirits," said Dr. David Adkinson, the surgeon who performed the operation on Friday.
Adkinson said Clinton began an early and limited therapy programme -- typical for all patients who have undergone such a procedure.
Adkinson said he slowly moved the president's right knee up and down several times -- a process that will be repeated daily during the early stages of Clinton's recovery.
"We'll see where it goes," Adkinson said of Clinton's recovery programme, which he said would be determined by the amount of discomfort the president could tolerate.
"He seems to tolerate (pain) and focus nicely," Adkinson said, adding that Clinton's progress would depend on the discomfort "he can stand."
Vice President Al Gore, who substituted for Clinton in delivering the president's weekly radio address to the nation, said during his remarks that "the president's doing great."

"He's resting comfortably and he'll be back on his feet, both of them, very soon," said Gore, who noted that Clinton was grateful to "all of you who have sent your prayers and best wishes for a speedy recovery."

Clinton caught his heel on a step at the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman early on Friday, causing his knee to buckle and tearing the quadriceps tendon connecting the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.

The president's injury forced him to cancel an appearance Saturday night at the annual Gridiron dinner, a formal white-tie event in which journalists lampoon the president and other prominent politicians. Clinton videotaped a message from the hospital for the dinner.
Clinton's right leg will be put in a leg brace and he was expected to rely on crutches for several months, his physicians said.

McCurry said there was no discussion of delaying or significantly altering Clinton's plans for a summit in Helsinki with Yeltsin -- whose own health has been more of a concern than that of the 50-year-old president.
A member of the medical team that treated Clinton was expected to accompany him to the summit, along with the physicans who routinely go on foreign presidential trips.
The accident forced postponement of a planned White House visit by Jordan's King Hussein that had been set for Tuesday.

On Monday Clinton planned a brief session with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Washington to prepare for the summit. He also expected to have a short exchange with Walter Mondale, the former U.S. vice president who is stepping down as American ambassador to Japan.
Clinton, however, will forgo the traditional St. Patrick's Day meeting with a senior Irish official. Prime Minister John Bruton, instead, will meet with Gore.
The accident also delayed the start of a two-week trip to Africa by Mrs. Clinton, who had planned to leave on Saturday. The first lady planned to depart Sunday afternoon.
